title: ‘Disastrous’: Inflation warnings on Hanson’s early access super plan
full_text:
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson’s plan to unlock compulsory super contributions for seven million renters and mortgage holders across the country could pile up to $26bn into the Australian economy, as economists warn the policy will only further fuel inflation.
In an appeal to cash-strapped households, One Nation would allow workers early access to a quarter of their compulsory contributions for up to three years, providing a tax-advantaged bump to Australians’ take-home pay.
Any withdrawals under the policy would receive the same tax treatment had they remained as super, meaning most Australians would be taxed at 15 per cent rather than their personal income tax rate.
Despite fervent warnings from economists and the superannuation sector, Senator Hanson, standing alongside Treasury spokesman Barnaby Joyce, declared the policy would be “inflation-neutral” and would be available to every Australian renting or servicing a mortgage.
“It’s neutral. So you won’t pump up inflation with it at all. Yes, it will affect seven million people that would be open to taking their super out. It won’t be inflationary,” she told reporters.
Under the proposal, employers would continue to pay the full 12 per cent to super funds, which would then be responsible for diverting 3 per cent of the contribution to participating households.
One Nation Leader Pauline Hanson and MP Barnaby Joyce unveiled a proposal to shake up the superannuation system, giving mortgage holders and renters a pay boost from future super contributions.
However, the policy was firmly repudiated by economists, the superannuation sector, unions and the government, which argued any cost-of-living relief delivered by the policy would be quickly eroded by inflationary pressures.
Economist Chris Richardson said the proposal encountered the same pitfalls as Labor’s 5 per cent deposit scheme and the “super for housing” policy the Coalition took to the last election.
“Australia’s problem is not a lack of money chasing housing. What we don’t have is enough housing. This just adds to the amount of money chasing housing,” he said.
“At the time of the 2025 federal election I described the housing policies on both sides as a dumpster fire of dumb … This is the same dumpster and the same fire, but it’s a bigger dumpster and a hotter fire.”
Deloitte Access Economics partner Stephen Smith said broadbased stimulus like the kind proposed by One Nation could only add to demand in the economy, putting further pressure on inflation.
“To the extent that governments or political parties want to help people, it needs to be extremely well-targeted. Energy subsidies to everyone, a fuel excise cut for everyone or 3 per cent additional wages for seven million Australians are not targeted,” he said.
Former Labor cabinet minister Joel Fitzgibbon believes One Nation’s new superannuation access plan will not be a good policy but a “popular one” among younger Australians.
“I think it’s a bad policy and should be knocked on the head relatively quickly.”
Centre for Independent Studies senior fellow Robert Carling, a former Treasury official, said while he was broadly supportive of the concept of an “opt-out” for compulsory superannuation contributions, the favourable tax treatment proposed by One Nation would invariably push up inflation.
“You would have a bigger take-up and there would be potential inflationary consequences … The concessional tax rate for super is not meant to apply to income that people can just draw out as they wish,” Mr Carling said.
The policy announcement also drew the ire of the superannuation sector, which warned it would be “economically disastrous” and erode the retirement savings of millions of Australians.
“Most Australians understand the basic economics. When you pour more money into a high-inflation economy, it makes everything more expensive. This proposal would not alleviate the cost of living; it would drive the cost of living higher,” Association of Superannuation Funds Australia CEO Mary Delahunty said.
“It is unfair to ask everyday working Australians to sacrifice their retirement savings to fix policy problems they didn’t cause, like inflation and the housing crisis.”
Super Members Council modelling showed a median full-time worker retiring $25,000 worse off having participated in the scheme for three years, leaving a couple with more than $50,000 less in savings.
“This would belt battlers – not help them – by damaging their super and their retirements and driving up both inflation and interest rates, which would make the cost-of-living pressures even worse, not better. We urge One Nation to ditch the idea,” Council CEO Misha Schubert said.
